Response Amplitude and Latency from a Multi-Basis Fit

Source: R/hrf_amplitude_latency.R
hrf_amplitude_latency.Rd

For every condition modelled with a multi-basis HRF (canonical plus temporal derivative, basis = "spmg2", or the quadrature pair fmrihrf::HRF_SPMGQ), combine the fitted basis coefficients into a response amplitude and a latency per voxel, using fmrihrf::amplitude_latency().

The canonical coefficient alone underestimates a response that peaks earlier or later than the canonical HRF, so condition differences in it mix amplitude with timing. The coefficients of a time-shifted response trace a known curve in coefficient space; each voxel's coefficients are matched to the nearest direction on that curve, which gives its latency, and their size along that direction gives the amplitude.

Usage

hrf_amplitude_latency(
  object,
  term = NULL,
  shifts = seq(-4, 4, by = 0.05),
  method = c("curve", "boost"),
  min_fit = 0
)

Arguments

object

A fitted fmri_lm object.

term

Optional character vector of term tags (as in fmridesign::design_colmap()) to restrict the result to. By default every event term with at least two basis functions is used.

shifts

Candidate latencies in seconds (positive = later than the canonical response). Estimates are limited to this range.

method

"curve" (default) matches coefficients to the shift curve and returns amplitude and latency. "boost" returns the derivative-boosted amplitude of Calhoun et al. (2004) and no latency.

min_fit

Voxels whose coefficients match the shift curve with a cosine below this value get NA (default 0).

Value

An object of class hrf_amplitude_latency: a list with numeric matrices amplitude, latency (seconds) and fit (cosine between the coefficients and the matched curve point), each with one row per voxel and one column per condition, plus conditions, a data frame giving each column's term, condition and basis. latency and fit are NA for method = "boost".

Details

Coefficients are matched in the metric of the basis functions' Gram matrix, which is appropriate for well-separated events; with heavily overlapping responses the estimates remain consistent but are not the most efficient, and a response that is shifted by several seconds is only approximately spanned by the basis, so part of it can be absorbed by neighbouring regressors. Latency is relative to the model's own timing: it includes any offset between the event onsets and the acquisition times assumed by the sampling frame. Latency is poorly determined where the amplitude is near zero, so mask the latency map (for example with a test on the amplitude) before interpreting it. The summaries are non-linear in the coefficients and have no closed-form standard error here: take the per-subject maps to a group analysis.

This function needs an fmrihrf that provides amplitude_latency().

References

Calhoun, V. D., Stevens, M. C., Pearlson, G. D., & Kiehl, K. A. (2004). fMRI analysis with the general linear model: removal of latency-induced amplitude bias by incorporation of hemodynamic derivative terms. NeuroImage, 22(1), 252-257. doi:10.1016/j.neuroimage.2003.12.029

Henson, R. N. A., Price, C. J., Rugg, M. D., Turner, R., & Friston, K. J. (2002). Detecting latency differences in event-related BOLD responses: application to words versus nonwords and initial versus repeated face presentations. NeuroImage, 15(1), 83-97. doi:10.1006/nimg.2001.0940

Liao, C. H., Worsley, K. J., Poline, J.-B., Aston, J. A. D., Duncan, G. H., & Evans, A. C. (2002). Estimating the delay of the fMRI response. NeuroImage, 16(3), 593-606. doi:10.1006/nimg.2002.1096

Examples

# \donttest{
if (exists("amplitude_latency", asNamespace("fmrihrf"))) {
  set.seed(1)
  events <- data.frame(
    onset = seq(4, 280, by = 16),
    condition = factor(rep(c("A", "B"), 9)),
    run = 1
  )
  # Simulate one voxel in which B peaks 1.5 s later than A
  time <- fmrihrf::samples(fmrihrf::sampling_frame(150, TR = 2))
  resp <- function(on) as.numeric(fmrihrf::evaluate(fmrihrf::regressor(on), time))
  y <- 100 + resp(events$onset[events$condition == "A"]) +
    resp(events$onset[events$condition == "B"] + 1.5) + rnorm(150, sd = 0.02)
  dset <- matrix_frame(cbind(y), TR = 2, run_length = 150, event_table = events)
  fit <- fmri_lm(onset ~ hrf(condition, basis = "spmg2"), block = ~ run,
                 dataset = dset)
  al <- hrf_amplitude_latency(fit)
  al$amplitude
  al$latency
}
# }
